## The Old Model of Toughness

Toughness is commonly associated with grit, stoicism, emotional control, perseverance, and playing through pain. Among 160 elite athletes, perseverance ranked highest. The traditional image is someone overcoming adversity through discipline and suffering: an athlete returning after a dislocated shoulder, Craig MacTavish playing without a helmet, a wounded military hero, or a mother enduring discomfort for her child. This often becomes the image of a physically dominant, emotionally impervious man.

Bobby Knight embodied this model. Across five decades and three universities, he won more than 900 games, reached five Final Fours, and won three NCAA championships. His undefeated 1976 Indiana team remains unmatched. Knight defined toughness as “Being able to overcome obstacles. You can’t feel sorry for yourself.” His pressing defense demanded discipline and perseverance, but his methods included humiliating “soft” players with tampons, abusive tirades, displaying feces-covered toilet paper, and choking a player at practice. His toughness meant showing no weakness, bulldozing obstacles, and using fear to establish authority and control.

## Demandingness Without Support

Diana Baumrind classified parenting according to **responsiveness**—attunement, support, and fostering individuality and self-regulation—and **demandingness**—expectations, supervision, discipline, and confronting disobedience. Low demandingness with high responsiveness produces permissiveness; high demandingness with low responsiveness produces authoritarian parenting. Authoritarian parents rely on fear, threats, punishment, and “You need to do (this) because I said so.” In one study of more than 1,000 parents, only 31 percent of authoritarian parents said they should “love their child unconditionally”; another found that 81 percent of Americans thought parents were too soft.

The problem is not expectations or punishment themselves, but an imbalance between demands and support. The “just right” pattern combines high expectations with warmth, care, and understanding. The same distinction applies to coaching, workplaces, and leadership, where demandingness is often retained while responsiveness is discarded.

This confusion turns toughness into callousness: thick skin, suppressed emotion, hidden vulnerability, and machismo. Youth programs may use laps, burpees, insults, or vomiting workouts simply to “toughen up.” In *Until It Hurts*, Mark Hyman found parents defending workouts that made eleven-year-olds vomit: “The stern approach is necessary for children to get in touch with their inner lacrosse warrior.” Slogans such as “man up,” “stop being a pussy,” and “There’s no crying in baseball!” reinforce the belief that toughness requires masculine bravado, although research suggests women quietly handle pain better than men.

## The Costs of Fake Toughness

On May 29, 2018, nineteen-year-old University of Maryland football player Jordan McNair began cramping and showing profound fatigue during a ten-sprint conditioning workout. Coaches and trainers told others to “get him the [expletive] up” and “drag his [expletive] across the field.” After he complained of cramps, 34 minutes passed before he was removed and another 28 before 911 was called; 1 hour and 28 minutes elapsed between his final sprint and the ambulance’s arrival. McNair died two weeks later from heatstroke. The tragedy showed the danger of confusing ordinary discomfort with physiological distress.

Extreme “toughening” workouts have also produced rhabdomyolysis, in which damaged muscle products enter the bloodstream and overburden the kidneys; severe cases can be fatal. B. David Ridpath described conditioning intended not to improve fitness but to make athletes suffer, sometimes to “weed out a few to open some scholarship slots.” Authoritarian styles produce psychological costs as well: lower independence, aggression, substance abuse, risky behavior, burnout, emotional exhaustion, and fear of failure. Among more than 1,200 parents, authoritarian parenting was linked to substantially more child misbehavior; in the Israeli military, people raised in authoritarian homes adapted worse than those from nurturing environments.

Fear creates compliance rather than self-direction. An athlete punished with exercise may work harder only to avoid punishment, not to improve or pursue an internal goal. Such training can create fragile, dependent people who function only when an authority figure is present—like teaching swimming by throwing children into the deep end.

## Redefining Toughness

Fake toughness is control- and power-driven, developed through fear, fueled by insecurity, and based on appearance over substance. Real toughness means experiencing discomfort or distress, paying attention, creating space, and taking thoughtful action. It involves navigating discomfort rather than automatically bulldozing through it: sometimes going through it, around it, under it, or waiting until it passes.

Pete Carroll illustrates this alternative. After losing his NFL job in the 1990s, he stopped imitating other coaches. He encourages meditation and yoga, may shift a heated meeting to ring toss, and turns mistakes into positives. Yet he is one of only three coaches to win both an NCAA championship and a Super Bowl. His difficult “always compete” practices aim to give players skills for handling adversity: “Teaching guys how to feel confident enough to believe in what they’ve been prepared to do and believing what they can do and they go out there and do it.” Real toughness replaces control with autonomy, fear with inner drive, rigidity with flexibility, and insecurity with quiet confidence.

A 2008 Eastern Washington study of nearly 200 basketball players and coaches found that the “keys” to mental toughness did not lie in “autocratic, authoritarian, or oppressive” leadership, but in trust and inclusion, humility, and service. Comparable humanistic coaches include Don Shula, Bill Walsh, Tony Dungy, John Wooden, Dean Smith, Brad Stevens, and Mike D’Antoni, who said, “We keep it positive here.”

## The Author’s Turning Point

The author’s search began during the Don Bowden Mile, a 1,609-meter race in which seven runners—including six from California and the author from Houston—were pursuing a four-minute mile. At 900 meters, unfamiliar neck tightness and a high-pitched gasp shattered his focus. Less than 100 meters later he could not inhale, stopped, and collapsed. After numerous tests and half a dozen specialists, Dr. Stephen Miles diagnosed **paradoxical vocal cord dysfunction (VCD)**: vocal cords that should open during inhalation instead shut reflexively and block the airway. Stress and “strong emotions” can trigger a hyperresponsive larynx, while panic worsens the symptoms.

His habitual strategy—pushing until exhaustion, sometimes vomiting after races—made the problem worse. To race again, he had to relax and keep his breathing, neck, and mind steady precisely when discomfort peaked. Toughness therefore meant noticing and navigating signals, not suppressing them or forcing the body onward.

The chapter introduces four pillars: **Ditch the Facade, Embrace Reality; Listen to Your Body; Respond Instead of React; and Transcend Discomfort.** Toughness is a learnable toolkit, not a rare trait reserved for the talented: “Real toughness is experiencing discomfort or distress, leaning in, paying attention, and creating space to take thoughtful action. It’s navigating discomfort to make the best decision you can.”

At 2:00 a.m., someone may remain on the couch watching television because inertia makes continuing easier than moving. Such apathy can signal an “inner crisis of hope”: without something important to pursue, action loses its force. An infomercial promising to solve every problem and make every dream come true exploits this condition. Its claims feel personal because they describe universal experiences—powerlessness, guilt, loneliness, suffering, and the sense of having lost something without knowing what. Absorbed in private pain, people forget that it is common and mistake a generalized account of the human condition for intimate insight.

The promise reaches the Feeling Brain’s need for hope; the Thinking Brain then rationalizes an absurd claim because the person wants it to be true. The seller presents himself as someone who was “once just as fucked as you” but found a way out, offering permanent fulfillment for “one low price.” This becomes the chapter’s central metaphor: religion organizes hope, values, emotional attachment, and collective action.

Religions create communal hope. Shared values produce a network effect: hope is amplified, group validation makes people feel important and worthy, and the Uncomfortable Truth seems farther away. Groups can make individuals feel understood, loved, and paradoxically in control despite having little actual control. Yet access to the Feeling Brain also makes groups suggestible, impulsive, and irrational—capable of becoming “murderous, angry mobs.” The system has six steps: sell hope, choose a faith, invalidate criticism, establish ritual and sacrifice, promise heaven while delivering hell, and profit from devotion.

## 1. Sell Hope to the Hopeless

In 2005, the author encountered the LaRouche Youth Movement (LYM) in Boston. Students displayed 9/11 photographs captioned “America Deserved It,” Dick Cheney with devil’s horns and “Mass Murderer,” and George W. Bush with a Hitler mustache. Founded by far-left ideologue Lyndon LaRouche, the LYM claimed that the international order was corrupt, the Iraq War enriched Bush’s friends, and terrorism and mass shootings were government efforts to control the population; years later it made comparable accusations about Obama.

Its effective message was “It’s not your fault.” Blame shifted from parents, professors, college, and government to the vague “system”; overthrowing it would end war, suffering, and injustice. Hope requires three things: a better future represented by values, a sense of capability or self-control, and a community sharing and supporting those values. Young adulthood is especially receptive because people must choose identities and values, manage themselves without constant authority, and find a community. LaRouche supplied an explanation for fear and aimlessness, a supposed method of changing the world, and belonging.

The author’s argument with the students illustrates that values cannot be changed through reason alone, but through experience. He answered an invitation to remain “open-minded” with Carl Sagan’s line, “I think your mind is so open your brain fell out!” Both sides felt smart; no minds changed. People are most impressionable when existing values fail. Loss of spiritual faith can redirect devotion toward a worldly God; loss of family toward race, creed, or nation; and loss of faith in government toward extremist ideology. Missionaries historically preached to poor and destitute populations because desperate people are receptive to promises of sustenance and meaning. Jim Jones recruited homeless and marginalized minorities with a socialist version of Christianity; Jesus and Buddha likewise preached to the poor, downtrodden, and enslaved. Social media makes recruitment easier, but anger alone is insufficient: followers need a semi-coherent vision of a greater cause and the winning side of history.

## 2. Choose Your Faith and God Value

Faith is unavoidable because evidence and science concern past experience while hope concerns the future. People pay mortgages because they trust money, credit, and banks; tell children to study because they believe education matters; pursue health because they believe longevity is worthwhile; and act as though happiness, love, work, and existence matter. Even nihilism rests on faith that nothing is more important than anything else. The question is not whether one has faith, but what one believes.

The Feeling Brain’s highest value becomes the “God Value,” the lens through which all others are interpreted. A person whose God Value is money evaluates family, love, prestige, politics, and anxiety monetarily; someone whose God Value is love rejects conflict and division. Jesus Christ, Muhammad, or the Buddha may serve as a God Value, as may personal pleasure and empowerment (narcissism) or another person (codependence). The codependent organizes behavior around pleasing, fixing, or saving a narcissist whose God Value is himself, producing a mutually reinforcing but unhealthy relationship.

Evidence does not determine values: evidence belongs to the Thinking Brain, while values are selected by the Feeling Brain and cannot be verified beyond doubt. If a meteorite killed half a town, a traditional religious person might see punishment for sin, an atheist evidence against a benevolent God, a hedonist a reason to party, and a capitalist an opportunity to develop meteorite-defense technology. Evidence serves the God Value unless evidence itself becomes the highest value—the basis of science, which the author calls “arguably the best thing we’ve ever done as a species.”

The chapter distinguishes three religions by their God Values:

- **Spiritual religions** draw hope from supernatural realities and promise improvement beyond this life: Christianity, Islam, Judaism, animism, and Greek mythology. They are difficult to establish but durable, since supernatural claims are nearly impossible to disprove and can make followers willing to die.
- **Ideological religions** draw hope from the natural world and claim that collective adoption of beliefs will improve this life: capitalism, communism, environmentalism, liberalism, fascism, and libertarianism. They are more testable but still depend on social constructions, faith, and generalizing limited evidence across complex populations. Racism and sexism persist through ignorance as well as malice because they provide explanatory structures and hope.
- **Interpersonal religions** draw hope from other people: romantic partners, children, sports heroes, political leaders, celebrities, families, and communities. They are easiest to form because people commonly surrender self-worth to another person.

Spiritual religions flourished when plagues, wars, slavery, and deprivation left little prospect of material improvement; afterlife rewards made suffering meaningful and held society together. Ideologies seek salvation in this life but compete as “isms.” Sports illustrate interpersonal religion: arbitrary rules make a field meaningful and deify or demonize athletes such as Ted Williams. Politics grants authority and virtue to leaders, while fandoms around Will Smith, Katy Perry, or Elon Musk offer hope through future films, songs, or inventions. Families and romantic relationships function as “mini-churches,” though modern civilization has often displaced intimate tribes with nationalist and internationalist ideologies.

## 3. Protect the Faith

A religion protects itself with a self-reinforcing us-versus-them dichotomy. “If you don’t support the war, then you support the terrorists”; anyone criticizing feminism is sexist, capitalism a Communist, or a president a traitor; anyone preferring Kobe Bryant to Michael Jordan supposedly understands no basketball and therefore has no valid opinion. Such formulas end discussion before followers question their beliefs and provide a common enemy. Followers become those who “get it” versus those who will destroy the world; nonbelievers must be demonized as evil.

Conspiracy theories intensify the structure: vaccines supposedly cause autism because medical companies want to destroy families; pro-choicers are Satan’s soldiers; climate change is a Chinese plot to weaken the United States. Common enemies turn pain into a crusade and sustain hope, although fear and self-righteousness can produce destructive behavior.

## 4. Ritual and Sacrifice

Rituals make values tangible because people cannot think their way into valuing something; they must live and experience it. Sunday clothes signal respect for the church community and membership in the “us.” Robes at weddings, graduations, funerals, court hearings, baptisms, surgeries, and sermons signal status and importance. Repeated symbolic actions connect people to the past, embody narratives, and reinforce identity: communion represents Christ’s sacrifice; national parades, flags, and fireworks represent a country’s history; couples’ gifts, anniversaries, and habits reaffirm their private religion.

Rituals often involve sacrifice because humans are guilt-ridden. Keeping an unreturnable wallet containing $100 produces guilt because something beneficial was received without being deserved. More fundamentally, people exist without knowing why or what they did to deserve life: this “inherent guilt of consciousness” is central to spiritual religion. Ancient sacrifices repaid that perceived debt, sometimes through human sacrifice; later, symbolic sacrifices such as Jesus’s allowed salvation without continual killing. Prayer functions as guilt alleviation—gratitude for existence combined with confession. Ideologies direct guilt toward national or social service, while interpersonal religions turn sacrifice into loyalty and romance through vows, rings, gifts, anniversaries, and mundane acts such as “wiping the piss off the floor when I miss the toilet.”

## 5. Promise Heaven, Deliver Hell

The more perfect salvation a religion promises, the more followers fail to attain it. Failure produces self-blame and guilt, increasing obedience. In a pyramid scheme, someone buys unwanted products, fails to recruit others, sees that the person at the top owns a Ferrari, and concludes that the failure is personal. Motivational seminars use music, chants, and slogans such as “Winners never give up! Losers believe it won’t work for them!” The same cycle appears in fitness, diets, political activism, self-help, financial planning, and family obligations: promised satisfaction remains out of reach, so followers are told to do more.

Human pain is a game of Whac-A-Mole. One pain may lessen or change shape, but another appears because pain is part of human nature. Leaders who claim to eliminate suffering remain in business by blaming followers or an enemy. If a leader solved every problem, followers would have no reason to follow. No religion produces permanent bliss; no country is entirely fair and safe; no philosophy solves everyone’s problems; true equality and freedom require trade-offs; and no relationship erases the guilt of existing. There are no final solutions, only stopgaps, incremental improvements, and “slightly better forms of fuckedness.” Hope requires accepting this rather than fleeing from it.

## 6. Prophet for Profit—and the Corruption of Success

Once followers are attached, a leader can extract money, labor, sex, land, political power, or lives. Authority defines what is ethical, right, and righteous. Yet everyone participates in religion broadly understood: adopting values, performing rituals, sacrificing, drawing us-versus-them boundaries, and relying on faith. Support networks are necessary to realize any vision; it “takes an army.” Religions compete for resources, and those whose value hierarchies use labor and capital most effectively spread, stabilize, and become foundations of culture.

Success creates corruption when a religion’s God Value shifts from its founding principles to preserving the organization and its power. This organizational narcissism explains the movement from Jesus to the Crusades, Marxism to the gulags, and a wedding chapel to divorce court. The corruption weakens the established religion and creates conditions for a newer, reactionary one to replace it.

Success is therefore more precarious than failure: the more one gains, the more one can lose, and experiencing a hope reveals its flaws and sacrifices. The final paradox is that “the only thing that can ever truly destroy a dream is to have it come true.”

Spiritual religions endured partly because most historical people had little prospect of material improvement. Plagues, wars, slavery, and pervasive deprivation made afterlife rewards a way to make suffering meaningful and hold society together. Their supernatural claims are nearly impossible to disprove, and their promise of reward after death can make followers willing to die. Ideologies are more testable, but humans generalize limited evidence across vastly complex populations; racism and sexism persist through ignorance as well as malice because they provide adherents with an explanatory structure and hope. Interpersonal religions are visible in sports, where arbitrary rules give meaning to a field and deify or demonize athletes such as Ted Williams, and in politics, where populations grant authority and virtue to leaders. Families and romantic relationships function as “mini-churches,” though modern civilization has often displaced these intimate tribes with nationalist and internationalist ideologies.

A religion protects itself through a self-reinforcing “us-versus-them” dichotomy. Critics are reclassified as outsiders: “If you don’t support the war, then you support the terrorists”; anyone criticizing feminism is sexist; anyone criticizing capitalism is a Communist; anyone criticizing a president is a traitor; anyone preferring Kobe Bryant to Michael Jordan supposedly understands no basketball and therefore has no valid opinion about it.

Conspiracy theories intensify this structure: vaccines supposedly cause autism because medical companies want to destroy families; pro-choicers are Satan’s soldiers; climate change is a Chinese plot to weaken the U.S. Common enemies convert pain into a crusade and preserve hope, though the resulting fear and self-righteousness can produce destructive behavior.

More fundamentally, people exist without knowing why or what they did to deserve life. This “inherent guilt of consciousness” is central to spiritual religion. Ancient sacrifices offered a perceived repayment of that debt, sometimes through actual human sacrifice; later, symbolic sacrifices such as Jesus’s allowed salvation without continual killing. Prayer likewise functions as guilt alleviation: gratitude for existence combined with confession.

Ideologies direct guilt toward national or social service—protecting country and family on the right, serving society on the left. Interpersonal religions turn sacrifice into loyalty and romance: marriage vows, rings, gifts, anniversaries, and mundane acts such as “wiping the piss off the floor when I miss the toilet” make people feel deserving of love.

## Kant and Maturity

Immanuel Kant’s rigid routine—waking at five, writing for three hours, lecturing for four, eating at the same restaurant, walking the same route at 3:30, and sleeping at ten—made him seem mechanical. Yet from Königsberg he helped shape individual freedom, inherent human dignity, animal rights, aesthetics, the United Nations, Einstein’s theory of relativity, and modern moral philosophy. He argued that right and wrong transcend emotion and “Feeling Brain” judgments, seeking value that could survive without hope.

## Psychological Development

Children explore the world to learn what pleases and harms them. Touching a hot stove teaches that burning is bad; stealing ice cream teaches that an angry, punishing mother is undesirable. The deeper lesson is a value judgment: eating ice cream is better than being burned. The “Feeling Brain” thereby constructs an initial hierarchy of preferences, harms, and satisfactions.

Because there is too much world to experience directly, children replace particular experiences with rules. After encountering enough flames, they infer that all flames are dangerous; after repeated punishment, that stealing dessert is generally bad. Abstract values such as prudence, honesty, and fairness emerge. The adolescent can reason through if/then chains: ice cream is desirable, but stealing it angers parents and produces punishment, so the pleasure is not worth the consequences. She learns that actions affect others, desires must be negotiated, and social rules can produce later rewards.

This is cognitive growth, but adolescent values remain transactional. She works for money, calls her mother to avoid being yelled at, does homework to protect her future, or acts nice to avoid conflict. Everything becomes a bargain in which present pain is exchanged for future pleasure or avoidance of punishment. She may function materially while remaining dependent on approval, trying on clothes, speech, music, and social roles to gain acceptance. She is a more sophisticated child pursuing pleasure several moves ahead, but does not yet stand for anything outside herself.

Adulthood requires acting according to a principle because it is right, not because it produces a desired result. Honesty is an end in itself, not a strategy for gaining trust or avoiding trouble. An adolescent may claim to value honesty but lie, exaggerate, or become passive-aggressive when truth is costly; an adult remains honest because honesty is more important than personal satisfaction. Likewise, an adult loves without demanding a return. Adult values are unconditional: they cannot be obtained as means to another end.

Age does not determine maturity. The child avoids stealing ice cream because it feels bad; the adolescent because future punishment outweighs present pleasure; the adult because stealing is wrong even if she could get away with it. The difference is not what people do, but why.

## Why Development Stalls

Children transcend pleasure-and-pain values when those values fail. Good parenting supplies predictable consequences—punishing theft and rewarding appropriate behavior—so children learn that the world does not cater to their impulses. If this lesson is postponed, peers, workplaces, and society impose harsher penalties: the selfish person is shunned, ridiculed, or excluded.

Abuse also blocks development. When punishment is random, excessively harsh, or absent, the child cannot connect actions to reliable principles. Stealing ice cream may sometimes bring severe punishment and sometimes none, producing coping mechanisms rather than higher values. Thus abused and coddled children can reach adulthood with similar problems: both remain trapped in a childhood value system. Progress into adolescence requires trust that behavior produces predictable outcomes; without trustworthy institutions and leaders, social rules cannot guide behavior and it collapses into childish self-interest.

Trauma and neglect can likewise leave people stuck in adolescent bargaining. Someone bullied as a child may assume affection and respect must always be earned through performed roles—dressing, speaking, and acting correctly. Some become skilled at sensing what others want and supplying it. Because manipulation appears to work, they conclude that all relationships are transactions: life becomes “one big high school gymnasium.”

The way out is unconditional example. Parents and teachers teach trust by trusting, respect by respecting, and love by loving without forcing a return. Adults who bargain love for sex, loyalty for affection, or respect for obedience reproduce transactional values in the next generation. Unconditional action requires faith—not necessarily hope for a pleasant outcome, but willingness to do what is right despite pain, rejection, or betrayal. The boss who takes responsibility for employees’ mistakes, the mother who sacrifices for her child, and the friend who tells an upsetting truth exemplify virtues that “hold the world together.”

Religions traditionally aim at such unconditionality: Jesus’s forgiveness, the Buddha’s Noble Eightfold Path, and Muhammad’s perfect justice. Yet religions become human institutions and are corrupted by transactional and narcissistic motives. Enlightenment “ideological religions” removed spirituality and pursued measurable goals—happiness, reduced suffering, liberty, compassion, empathy, and equality—but repeated the same error. Bargaining for happiness destroys happiness; enforcing freedom negates freedom; imposing equality can undermine equality. Whatever becomes a “God Value,” pursued conditionally enough, can lead people to sacrifice human life and humanity itself.

## The Formula of Humanity

Kant sought value without hope. Consciousness, as far as we know, is uniquely capable of reasoning, choosing meaning, inventing purposes, improving systems, and directing existence. Rocks merely exist; consciousness can reorganize the universe and generate increasing complexity—from “twiddling sticks in a small cave” to digital realms connecting billions, and potentially, in another thousand years, reaching the stars. Therefore, the supreme value is the capacity that conceives value: consciousness and rational agency. Its preservation and growth, in ourselves and others, is the fundamental moral duty.

Kant called this “the Formula of Humanity”: “Act that you use humanity, whether in your own person or in the person of any other, always at the same time as an end, never merely as a means.” The principle moves people from adolescent bargaining to adult virtue. Hope is transactional: sacrifice something now for an imagined future reward. Unconditional action treats persons as ends in themselves without requiring a payoff.

The distinction between means and ends clarifies ordinary morality. Driving to Chipotle, buying gas, and paying for a double-meat burrito are means to eating it. If the burrito is wanted only to make one’s wife happy, it becomes a means to that higher end; if her happiness is sought only to obtain sex, treating the wife as a means becomes morally wrong. Lying manipulates another person’s conscious behavior to achieve one’s goal. Cheating treats other test-takers or rule-followers as means to personal success. Violence treats another person as a tool for political or personal ends.

The formula also explains virtue. Honesty is good because it does not treat people merely as means. Courage matters because refusing to act can treat oneself or others as means to avoiding fear. Humility matters because blind certainty turns others into instruments of one’s own ends. The principle requires neither future utopia nor supernatural faith: conscious will must be respected and protected in each moment.

Improvement therefore means cultivating self-respect, not merely maximizing happiness. Treating oneself as worthless, lying to oneself, or harming oneself is as ethically wrong as doing those things to others. Self-love and self-care are ethical obligations. Honesty with oneself improves honesty with others, which can encourage their maturation. The world changes not through mass conversion or an all-encompassing ideology, but through each person’s present dignity and conduct.

## The Modern Maturity Crisis

Democracy assumes that people are selfish and delusional, so it distributes power among interlocking institutions that prevent one person or group from dominating everyone else. Rights such as free speech, freedom of the press, privacy, and a fair trial institutionalize the Formula of Humanity by protecting individuals from being treated merely as means.

Democracy is threatened when a group elevates its own values above the system and replaces democratic restraint with another religion. Extremists are childish in refusing to negotiate, recognize competing interests, or appeal to principles above their desires; their authoritarianism reflects a longing for an all-powerful parent to make everything “all right.” Right-wing extremists may invoke “freedom” while seeking freedom from values, change, or marginalized people, and may destroy others’ freedom in its name. Left-wing extremists may invoke “equality” while trying to eliminate all pain, inferiority, and moral discomfort, even by causing pain and adversity.

The prominence of extremism may have many complicated, overlapping causes, but one possibility is deteriorating cultural maturity. The developed world faces less a crisis of material wealth than a crisis of character, virtue, and the relation between means and ends. The central political conflict is increasingly not simply right versus left, communism versus capitalism, or freedom versus equality, but maturity versus immaturity: impulsive values on both sides versus the compromising, principled values needed to treat human beings as ends.

## Organizing: The Right Buckets

A trustworthy external system lets the mind release lower-level remembering and focus on broader horizons. Organization means that “where something is matches what it means to you”: reference goes with reference, and a call reminder goes where call reminders belong. Clarification comes first; as inputs are processed, lists and groupings evolve. The core distinctions remain stable, but the best structure may change with work and life.

The seven categories are **Projects**, **Project Support Material**, **Calendar actions and information**, **Next Actions lists**, **Waiting For**, **Reference material**, and **Someday/Maybe**. They must remain visually, physically, and psychologically distinct. Mixing reference with reading material makes a stack psychologically invisible; putting day-specific actions on Next Actions weakens trust in the calendar; leaving inactive projects on Projects undermines its action-generating focus; and mixing Waiting For with personal actions causes repetitive rethinking. Once inputs are clarified, lists and folders suffice: lists track projects, Someday/Maybes, and actions, while paper or digital folders hold reference and support material. Lists are inventories, not priority rankings; priorities are chosen during review as circumstances change.

## Action Reminders

Processing an in-tray may produce **twenty to sixty or seventy or more** pending actions, delegated items, and possible calendar or Someday/Maybe entries. Group them so they can be reviewed according to time, energy, tools, location, and situation.

The calendar is for actions or information that must occur on a specific day or time: “10:00–11:00 meet with Jim” or “Call Rachel Tuesday to see if she got the proposal.” It should show only the “hard landscape.” An action that could move from Monday to Tuesday belongs on a Next Actions list, not the calendar. This exactness makes the calendar trustworthy and leaves most actions in the “as soon as possible” category.

Organize as-soon-as-possible actions by context—tool, location, or situation. Common lists include **Calls, At Computer, Errands, At Office, At Home, Anywhere, Agendas**, and **Read/Review**. The number depends on action volume and changing contexts: one list may suffice for **twenty-five** actions, but **fifty or a hundred** makes a single list require repeated sorting. Context lists reduce switching costs and exploit activity “modes.” Calls should include phone numbers where possible. Allen keeps **Online** separate from At Computer because, when flying without Wi-Fi, he can trust that At Computer actions do not require the Web.

Errands can combine “Get stock certificates from bank deposit box,” “Pick up suit at the tailor,” and “Buy flowers for Robyn at the florist”; a hardware-store item may carry a sublist. Location-based reminders are useful only as an option within a rigorously reviewed system, not as a sole system. At Office and At Home hold location-specific actions, with variants such as “At Office A,” “At Office B,” or “At Starbucks.”

**Agendas** collect topics for particular people or recurring meetings—bosses, partners, assistants, children, attorneys, advisers, or staff meetings—and may require **three to fifteen** lists. **Read/Review** holds material requiring more than two minutes, often in a tray or portable folder; digital equivalents include **Review/Watch** or **Surf Web**. It must contain only material genuinely intended for later attention, or it becomes numbing.

**Waiting For** tracks deliverables for which another person is responsible, such as theater tickets, an office scanner, or a client’s approval. It is a trigger, not usually an action reminder: review it and decide whether follow-up is needed. Record both the request date and agreed due date. Items can move between categories: request a vendor proposal, place it on Waiting For, review it via Read/Review or At Computer, send it to a boss, and return it to Waiting For.

Usually process the originating e-mail, paper, voice mail, or meeting notes and put the reminder on the appropriate list. Exceptions include magazines in Read/Review, bills in **Bills to Pay**, receipts in **Receipts to Process**, or standardized customer requests in an actionable tray. This works only if the container is reliably reviewed, and documents should be separated by next action rather than document type.

Actionable e-mail may remain in the e-mail system. **@ACTION** holds longer-than-two-minute actions and **@WAITING FOR** delegated requests or expected responses; a cc: or bcc: copy can preserve a delegated request. If undealt-with mail is no more than **one screenful**, leaving it in “in” may suffice. Emptying “in” means deleting, filing, doing quick responses, and moving actionable and waiting items—not completing everything. Distributed reminders are safe only when every category is reviewed; off-screen digital data can disappear as a prompt.

## Projects and Support Material

A project is any commitment or desired outcome requiring more than one action, including “look into getting a dog for our kids” and “find a good tailor.” The **Projects list** is a complete index of open loops, not a priority ranking, plan, or action list: one cannot do a project, only its action steps. Regular review, especially the Weekly Review, confirms a current next action for every project, prevents omissions, supports workload evaluation, and enables negotiation of commitments.

Hidden projects emerge from current activities, higher-horizon interests and commitments, and problems, process improvements, or creative opportunities. A next action such as “Call Mario re: the fund-raising event” may imply “Finalize the fund-raiser.” “When is a problem a project? Always”: treating something as a problem assumes a possible resolution or at least research. Examples include “Look into improving Frederick’s relationship with his school,” “Resolve situation with landlord and building maintenance,” and “Get closure on compensation dispute with business partner.”

One master list usually works best, though Personal/Professional, Projects—Delegated, Projects—Presentations, sales relationships, or major areas of focus are acceptable if all are reviewed. Subprojects may be separate entries or support material. For “Finish new home upgrades,” “Upgrade the kitchen” may wait for “Assess and upgrade home electrical system,” while “Finalize the patio” can proceed independently. During Allen’s move from California to Europe, “Move to Amsterdam” became fifteen projects, including “Set up Dutch bank accounts” and “Finalize artwork storage in Santa Barbara.”

Project support materials are resources for thinking and doing, not reminders. The project belongs on Projects; next actions and Waiting For items belong on their own lists. Plans and notes may be stored in digital notes, e-mail folders such as **“Johnson Partnership—Active”** and **“Johnson Partnership—Archive,”** paper folders, or notebook pages, but should be reviewed with the project. Digital abundance can scatter information across unlinked locations, so project-list review and clearing stale notes are essential.

## Reference and Future Options

Nonactionable material comprises **reference**, future possibilities, and trash. Reference is a library, not a reminder system. Once action is separated from it, its size is mainly logistical. Allen keeps restaurant information under “Locales—London—Restaurants,” with one topic populating hundreds of folders and subfolders. A topic needing more than **fifty folders and/or major documents** may deserve its own section or database. There is no perfect reference architecture: balance value, retrieval needs, and maintenance cost, then reassess.

**Someday/Maybe** holds options such as “Learn Spanish,” “Get Marcie a horse,” “Climb Mt. Washington,” “Write a mystery novel,” and “Get a vacation cottage,” as well as trips, skills, hobbies, books, recipes, gifts, and ideas. It permits creative imagining without commitment; Allen says learning the flute and sailing in the open ocean began there. Move optional active projects to it when they will not receive attention for several months. Avoid vague “Hold and Review” piles: without consistent review they become catchalls containing trash, reference, reading, calendar items, and unclarified actions.

The calendar can hold future project triggers, possible events, and decision catalysts. Deciding not to decide is acceptable only with a trusted future reminder. A **tickler file** is a physical “three-dimensional version of a calendar,” requiring **forty-three folders**: thirty-one numbered daily folders and twelve monthly folders. Each day’s folder is emptied into the in-tray and refiled at the back; monthly folders advance similarly. It must be checked daily, including before travel, or trust collapses.

## Organizing Means Matching Meaning to Place

A trusted organization system lets the mind release lower-level remembering and focus intuitively on broader horizons. This requires the physical system to be more reliable than the mental one. ## Sorting, Not Development

In 1954, Texas A&M coach Paul “Bear” Bryant took nearly one hundred players to Junction, Texas, for a ten-day camp intended to “separate the quitters from the keepers.” Heat, drought, poor facilities, and brutal practices reduced the group to twenty-seven to thirty-five: “We went out there in two buses and came back in one.” Yet the team went 1–9. Only eight survivors played on the 9–0 1956 team, whose central players—Heisman winner John David Crow, quarterback Jim Wright, and tackle Charlie Krueger—were freshmen who had not attended Junction. A&M also improved by acquiring blue-chip recruits; Bryant acknowledged that alumni “paid a few boys.”

The camp therefore sorted more than it toughened. Future NFL players Fred Broussard and Joe Boring quit, as did Foster “Tooter” Teague, later a Navy TOPGUN pilot, Silver Star recipient, USS Kitty Hawk commander, and Soviet MiG test pilot. Injury, priorities, and football’s importance—not innate toughness—helped determine who stayed. Bryant later apologized, saying he did not know whether his method was right.

## What the Military Teaches

Navy SEAL “Hell Week” similarly sorted people able to function under wartime stress; it was not designed to develop toughness. Extreme stress can produce dissociation—amnesia, depersonalization, or derealization. Research found symptoms in 96 percent of soldiers; 65 percent had “lost track of what was going on,” and all but two of ninety-four felt they viewed the world “through a fog.”

SERE (Survival, Evasion, Resistance, and Escape) develops capacity through sequence: classroom instruction, evasion, then simulated detention. Its 652-page manual covers medicine, camouflage, fire making, “river hydraulics,” and psychological coping. Stress inoculation requires learning coping skills before practicing them under manageable stress; overwhelming exposure is counterproductive. RAND’s 2014 recommendations emphasized confidence, goal setting, attention and arousal control, imagery, self-talk, compartmentalization, and mastering these before stress exposure.

Resilient soldiers appraise stress as challenge, use flexible coping, process internal signals without reacting, and regulate physiology. Toughness is not freedom from discomfort: high performers still want to quit. The sequence is **feel → inner debate → urge → decision**. Because the brain reduces uncertainty, it may quit to turn the unknown into the known. Toughness means tolerating uncertainty long enough to guide, rather than reflexively obey, the response.

## Small Habits Compound

In 2003, Dave Brailsford redirected British Cycling through “the aggregation of marginal gains”: breaking cycling into components and improving each by 1 percent. The team redesigned seats, rubbed alcohol on tires, regulated muscle temperature, used biofeedback, tested fabrics in a wind tunnel, optimized massage gels, taught riders hand-washing, individualized pillows and mattresses, and painted the team truck white to reveal dust. Five years later, Britain won 60 percent of cycling gold medals at the 2008 Beijing Olympics; in 2012 it set nine Olympic and seven world records. Bradley Wiggins became the first British Tour de France winner, followed by Chris Froome’s victories in 2013, 2015, 2016, and 2017. From 2007 to 2017, British cyclists won 178 world championships and sixty-six Olympic or Paralympic gold medals.

A 1 percent daily improvement compounds to nearly thirty-seven times better in a year; a 1 percent decline approaches zero. Habits are “the compound interest of self-improvement”: initially negligible effects become decisive over years. Like an airplane changing course 3.5 degrees from Los Angeles, daily choices produce different destinations. Outcomes—weight, knowledge, net worth, or clutter—are lagging measures of repeated habits, so trajectory matters more than present results. Good habits make time an ally; bad habits make it an enemy.

## Delayed Progress

Progress often stays invisible until a threshold: an ice cube remains unchanged from twenty-five to thirty-one degrees, then melts at thirty-two. Cancer can remain undetectable for 80 percent of its life; bamboo builds roots for five years before rising ninety feet in six weeks. This “Valley of Disappointment,” or “Plateau of Latent Potential,” stores effort before breakthrough. The San Antonio Spurs display Jacob Riis’s reminder that the hundred-and-first hammer blow succeeds because of all that preceded it. Mastery therefore requires persistence through delayed results.

## Systems over Goals

Goals specify results; systems specify the processes producing them. Goals set direction, but systems make progress. Winners and losers often share goals—the British cyclists always wanted the Tour de France—so continuous improvement, not desire, differentiates outcomes. Achieving a goal creates only momentary change unless the underlying system changes: fixing inputs fixes outputs. Goals can postpone happiness, reduce success to an either-or outcome, and produce a yo-yo effect after achievement. Long-term progress requires endless refinement.

An atomic habit is a small, easy practice embedded in a larger system: like atoms, habits are building blocks of remarkable results. “You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.”

## AI and the Final Religion

In 1997 IBM’s Deep Blue defeated Garry Kasparov, then the world’s best chess player. A computer therefore needs both a powerful **Thinking Brain** for calculation and a “Feeling Brain”—algorithms that judge which positions are worth calculating.

Peter Heine Nielsen said, “I always wondered how it would be if a superior species landed on earth and showed us how they play chess. ## Pilecki and Heroism

At Auschwitz, more than 1.3 million people were systematically sorted, enslaved, tortured, and murdered over four years on an area slightly larger than Central Park. Witold Pilecki, a decorated veteran of the 1918 Polish-Soviet War, had settled into rural family life before Nazi Germany and the Soviet Union invaded Poland. Poland fell in little more than a month; the Soviets rounded up over a million Polish citizens, sending some to Siberian gulags and leaving others in mass graves.

After fighting both invaders, Pilecki helped form the Secret Polish Army in Warsaw. In 1940, suspecting Auschwitz held thousands of disappearing Polish officers, he volunteered to be arrested and sent there—the only man known to have voluntarily entered a Nazi concentration camp. He planned to organize Polish soldiers, coordinate a mutiny, and escape.

Auschwitz was worse than the resistance imagined. Prisoners were shot for minor infractions such as fidgeting or failing to stand straight; labor was endless and often deliberately pointless; and one-third of the men in Pilecki’s barracks died from exhaustion, pneumonia, or execution during his first month. By the end of 1940, he had created an espionage network, embedding messages in laundry baskets, building a transistor radio from spare parts and stolen batteries, transmitting plans to Warsaw, and organizing smuggling rings for food, medicine, and clothing. Over two years he developed a resistance unit with ranks, logistics, and outside communications, hoping to coordinate a revolt, overwhelm the undermanned guards, and release tens of thousands of Polish guerrillas.

The arrival of Jews transformed the scale of the horror. They came first in buses, then packed train cars, and were directed into renovated “shower” barracks, gassed, and burned. Pilecki reported that tens of thousands were being murdered each day, mostly Jews, and urged the resistance to liberate Auschwitz or at least bomb the gas chambers. His reports reached the Secret Polish Army, the Polish government-in-exile, Allied Command, Eisenhower, and Churchill, but all assumed he was exaggerating.

In 1943, realizing that no rescue was coming, Pilecki escaped. He faked illness, entered the camp hospital, claimed the bakery’s night shift, waited until 2:00 a.m., cut a telephone wire, opened a back door, changed into stolen civilian clothes, ran a mile to the river under fire, and navigated by the stars. After the war he spied on Poland’s Communist government, reporting Soviet infiltration, rigged elections, and atrocities. Offered escape to Italy, he stayed because a free, independent Poland was his source of hope. Captured in 1947, he was tortured for almost a year, telling his wife that “Auschwitz was just a trifle” by comparison. In a 1948 show trial he was convicted of espionage and treason and sentenced to death. His final statement said, “I have tried to live my life such that in the hour of my death I would feel joy rather than fear.”

Manson defines heroism as more than bravery, resilience, or clever maneuvering: it is “the ability to conjure hope where there is none,” to “strike a match to light up the void” and reveal a better world people did not know was possible. Heroes possess an unshaken philosophical “Why?”—a cause that makes action meaningful despite overwhelming circumstances. Modern culture has prosperity, peace, and convenience but lacks such a clear “Why,” and therefore needs hope.

## The Uncomfortable Truth and Hope

The Uncomfortable Truth is that everyone we love will die, almost nothing we do will matter beyond a small group of people for a brief time, and the universe does not care about our families, elections, careers, environmental disasters, or survival. Humans are “inconsequential cosmic dust” who imagine importance and invent purpose. Because meaninglessness is psychologically unbearable, we project importance onto the world; caring becomes evidence, to our minds, that life must matter.

Hope is the psyche’s primary stabilizing project. It needs hope “the way a fish needs water”: without belief that the future might improve, we spiritually die. The opposite of happiness is not anger or sadness, since those emotions show that something still matters and hope remains. It is hopelessness—resignation, indifference, and the belief that everything is fucked, so nothing is worth doing. Manson presents hopelessness as the root of mental suffering: anxiety is fear of a failed future, depression belief in a meaningless future, and delusion, addiction, or obsession an attempt to manufacture hope.

People maintain purpose through “hope narratives,” or before/after stories: the belief that the future can contain growth, improvement, or salvation and that actions can move us toward it. After his grandfather died, Manson decided to live so as to make him proud, imagining him as a “really nosy ghost.” This irrational “mini-religion of purpose” gave empty experiences meaning. Other narratives involve raising children, saving the environment, making money and owning a big boat, or improving a golf swing. They may rest on religion, evidence, intuition, or argument; their common structure is potential improvement plus a route toward it. Religion’s acknowledgment of uncertainty and demand for faith may help explain why religious people experience depression and suicide at lower rates than nonreligious people.

Manson presents the book itself as a hope narrative: he does not know whether it will help people, but believing it might gives his life meaning. The book begins with nihilism not to endorse it, but to construct a sustainable, benevolent hope grounded in reason and reality and capable of bringing people together.

## The Paradox of Progress

Materially, the modern world is safer, healthier, freer, wealthier, more educated, and less violent than earlier periods. Steven Pinker and Hans Rosling document declining violence, racism, sexism, discrimination, extreme poverty, war, and child mortality; increased rights, literacy, longevity, wealth, and internet access; and the eradication of many diseases. Yet depression and anxiety in U.S. young people have risen for eighty years and among adults for twenty; life satisfaction has declined since 1985; overdoses, loneliness, isolation, extremism, and social distrust have increased. Nearly half of Americans report feeling isolated, left out, or alone. When asked how many people they discussed important personal matters with, the most common answer changed from “three” in the 1980s to “zero” in 2006. The wealthier and safer a place is, the more likely its inhabitants are to commit suicide.

This is the paradox of progress: past improvements do not automatically create hope about the future. Hope concerns unsolved problems, not those already resolved; as the world improves, there is more to lose and less that feels guaranteed.

Hope requires three interdependent conditions: **control**, the sense that one can affect one’s fate; **values**, something important and worthwhile to pursue; and **community**, a group sharing those values and working toward them. Without community, values lose social meaning; without values, nothing seems worth pursuing; without control, pursuit feels powerless. Losing any one undermines the other two and destroys hope. The next chapters examine control, values, and community before returning to why people feel worse even as conditions improve.
